newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian minister works on as scandal swirls.
newsitem.headline: Russian minister works on as scandal swirls.

text.p: Russian Justice Minister Valentin Kovalyov, allegedly filmed taking a sauna in a gangland nightclub, was working at his office on Monday despite Sunday's announcement that he was to be suspended from his post.
"We have not received any instructions and the minister spent all day working as usual," a ministry spokesman said.

Meanwhile the affair was turning into a far more Byzantine business than a simple western-style sleaze scandal. Attention focused on the motives for the release of the video tape rather than on Kovalyov's purported role in it.

Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov, indicating he believed the tape was genuine, said it had been seized by police earlier this year when they arrested a Moscow banker for theft. He said its disclosure was an attempt to undermine the case.

The weekly newspaper Sovershenno Sekretno (Top Secret) last week published grainy snaps taken from a video which it said showed Kovalyov relaxing with naked women in September 1995 in the sauna of a nightclub frequented by Russian mafia gangsters.
Like Kulikov, the paper focused on the banker's alleged machinations, and all but ignored what the minister may or may not have been doing in the sauna.
Kovalyov, 53, is a member of the Kremlin's top-level Security Council. He asked President Boris Yeltsin on Saturday to take him off the job until he could clear his name.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin said on Sunday Kovalyov would be suspended and on Monday one of Chernomyrdin's deputies, Boris Nemtsov, said an investigation had been launched.

"At present, there is no talk of opening a criminal case against Kovalyov," chief state prosecutor Yuri Skuratov said on Monday in remarks broadcast on NTV television. "We have to check out all the circumstances."
He said the video might have been made public illegally while being used as part of a criminal inquiry.
Kulikov told NTV that allies of the banker were using the tape to discredit the police and destroy the case against him.

"People who felt that it looked like the person arrested in this case, from whom this tape was seized, was not going to be freed...put out this information to blame the Interior Ministry for apparently making the case collapse," the minister said.
Reactions to the affair, in a country where scandals about politicians' private lives are practically unknown, were supportive of Kovalyov, who said he had done nothing to be ashamed of.

Outspoken nationalist politician Vladimir Zhirinovsky, who boasts that he is a sex symbol, said: "Isn't it abhorrent to peer through keyholes? So what if some washes in some sauna somewhere? Kovalyov hasn't done any harm to anyone."
Nemtsov said jokingly: "I prefer to wash in the sauna." But he backed the view that the article was an invasion of privacy.

"The state has no right to climb into bed with the people, it has absolutely no right, and one would hope it would be the same the other way around," said Nemstov, one of the young ministers leading the government's new reform drive.
Interfax news agency said Kovalyov, who resigned from the Communist party on being made a minister in January 1995, was planning to sue the racy newspaper for breach of privacy.
